finding: Id-based dispatch survives outside the switch and the spec does not say so. buildRolePrompt (internal/cli/audit_roles.go:220) injects the CLAUDE.md '## Project Context' section only when `role == roleMaintainability`, and TestGenerateAuditPrompts_CLAUDEmdOnlyForMaintainability (audit_named_test.go:69) pins that behavior with NotContains assertions for the other roles. §4 requires the docs to state that 'no id is treated specially', and §2.1's stated observable consequence is that a role named `security` and an identically-authored role named anything else are equivalent — but after this change a role renamed away from `maintainability-conventions` silently loses a whole prompt section. Worse for testability: §6 item 2 is scoped to 'the same checklist item count and the same affected-files list', so it PASSES while the surviving id dispatch remains — the anti-regression guard is neutered by its own scope.

resolved.evidence: §2.3 added: buildRolePrompt no longer gates ## Project Context on the maintainability-conventions id; every shared-arm role receives it and spec-coverage does not. §2.8 item 4 states the fate of TestGenerateAuditPrompts_CLAUDEmdOnlyForMaintainability, and §7 item 2 was widened from item-count equality to full prompt equality modulo role id and output path, so the neutered-guard problem is closed.

suggestion: Decide and state the fate of the CLAUDE.md excerpt branch: keep it (then §4 must not claim 'no id treated specially' and §2.1 must carve it out as a documented exception), give it to every non-spec-coverage role, or drop it. Then widen §6 item 2 to assert prompt-body equality modulo the role name/output path — or add an explicit item asserting which prompt sections each role gets — and say what happens to TestGenerateAuditPrompts_CLAUDEmdOnlyForMaintainability.

finding: §2.1 removes id dispatch only from generateRoleAuditPrompts, but buildRolePrompt (internal/cli/audit_roles.go:220) still gates the '## Project Context' CLAUDE.md conventions excerpt on `role == roleMaintainability`. So after this release an identically-authored role still does NOT produce an identical prompt: the id `maintainability-conventions` silently receives up to 50 lines of project conventions that a role named anything else never sees. That is the same id-string magic the release exists to delete, and it is the expensive half — a custom conventions auditor named e.g. `house-style` audits without the project's conventions and returns wrong-convention findings, each of which costs a resolve round-trip and can block the 2-consecutive-clean audit convergence. §6 test 2 asserts only checklist item count and affected files, so it passes while the magic persists, and §4 would then have docs assert 'no id is treated specially', which would be untrue.

resolved.evidence: Same defect as the tester's surviving-id-dispatch finding, fixed together: §2.3 attaches the Project Context block to every non-spec-coverage role with the correctness rationale (a convention-blind auditor's findings each cost a resolve round-trip), and §7 item 2 now compares the whole prompt body so a residual id gate anywhere in prompt construction fails a test.

suggestion: Extend §2.1 to buildRolePrompt: the Project Context excerpt is either given to every non-spec-coverage role or to none (a fixed always-on block is the cheaper, more predictable choice). If it stays id-gated, say so explicitly in §2.1 and §4 and state why. Strengthen §6 test 2 to compare the full emitted prompt body modulo the role name, not just the checklist count.

finding: §6 names only two existing tests as staying green (items 5 and 8), but two behavioral tests encode the exact defect being removed and will FAIL: internal/cli/audit_routing_test.go:79 TestGenerateAuditPrompts_EmptyRoleOmitted asserts `security` is ABSENT from prompts when the only affected file is plain.go ("security role with no matching files is omitted") — under §2.1 security now always emits; and TestRouteChecklist_Disjoint:63-64 asserts `require.Len(t, secItems, 1, "only the auth-matching file")` — security now receives one item per code file (2). A reviewer cannot tell from §6 whether those assertions are meant to be inverted, rewritten, or deleted, and an implementer could 'fix' them by re-adding the heuristic. Also unaddressed: routeChecklist (internal/cli/audit_roles.go:31,54-55) still precomputes sec/maint from sel.Security/sel.Maintainability, so its three-value contract must change too — §2.1 never mentions routeChecklist.

resolved.evidence: §2.8 'Existing tests this change invalidates' added, naming each test and its new assertion: EmptyRoleOmitted inverts and becomes the §7.1 guard, RouteChecklist_Disjoint is rewritten against the new single return value, FilterFiles_Security and the security half of FilterFiles_Cap20 are deleted, the CLAUDEmd test is rewritten. §2.1 now also states routeChecklist's collapsed contract and the dropped secItems/maintItems parameters.

suggestion: Add a §6 item (or a subsection of §2.1) naming each existing test the change invalidates and its new expected assertion: TestGenerateAuditPrompts_EmptyRoleOmitted inverts to 'security IS emitted with one file_check item for plain.go' (making it the regression guard of §6 item 1), TestRouteChecklist_Disjoint's security item count becomes len(code files). State explicitly what routeChecklist returns after the change (spec + finding items only, with file_check items built per role inside the shared arm).

finding: The shared arm hands every non-spec-coverage role one file_check item per selected code file with no relevance filter — after §2.2 the `security` role gets 'Apply the security role rules to <path>' for files that may have nothing to do with security. The audit status enum is PASS/PARTIAL/FAIL only (internal/cli/audit_schema.go), evidence_file/evidence_lines are required for PASS, and `tp audit --record` counts every non-PASS row against the 2-consecutive-clean convergence. The spec never states the expected disposition for a file outside a role's lens, so sub-agents will plausibly return PARTIAL/FAIL ('cannot evaluate', 'no authorization code here'), each of which is a false blocker costing a fix-or-justify round-trip and an extra full audit round (N sub-agents each).

resolved.evidence: §2.2 added: a file with nothing in the role's domain is a PASS citing the inspected file, and that instruction is written into the expected_evidence fileCheckItems generates rather than left to sub-agent judgment; PARTIAL/FAIL stay reserved for a real defect. §7 item 7 pins the wording so the false-blocker path cannot reappear.

suggestion: State in §2.1 that a file containing nothing in the role's domain is a PASS citing the inspected file, and carry that into the emitted item text or expected_evidence produced by fileCheckItems (e.g. expected evidence 'inspect <path>; PASS if nothing in this role's domain appears'). Add a §6 test pinning the wording so the disposition is not left to sub-agent judgment.

finding: Item 3 is written as a conditional the spec never resolves: 'AuditFileInputs.HeadReader and GitHeadReader are removed when no other caller reads them; a caller that still needs file content at HEAD keeps them'. No deterministic assertion can be written from that — the acceptance depends on a fact the spec declines to state (the sole reader is internal/cli/audit.go:192, set purely for selectSecurity). Separately, the heuristic has TWO inputs — path substring AND the first 200 lines at HEAD — but §6 item 3 only exercises the path half (renaming a file). Removal of the content half (the HeadReader path exercised by TestFilterFiles_Security:79-96) has no test at all.

resolved.evidence: §2.4 item 3 replaced the conditional with the decided fact: HeadReader is read only by selectSecurity and assigned only in runAudit, so the field, its assignment and GitHeadReader are all removed, and AuditFileInputs keeps Universe/DiffStats/Deleted/TaskFiles. §7 item 4 added to cover the content half of the heuristic, which had no test.

suggestion: Replace the conditional with the fact: 'HeadReader is read only by selectSecurity via audit.go's inputs construction, so AuditFileInputs.HeadReader, its assignment in runAudit, and GitHeadReader are all removed.' Add a §6 item covering the content half: a file whose first lines contain `validate`/`auth` but whose path does not now receives exactly the same treatment as any other code file (previously it alone reached the security list).

finding: Item 3 — '`AuditFileInputs.HeadReader` and `GitHeadReader` are removed when no other caller reads them; a caller that still needs file content at HEAD keeps them' — states a condition instead of a fact, so both removing and keeping them satisfy the acceptance and no task can be verified against it. In the current tree the condition is already decidable: HeadReader is read only by selectSecurity (auditfiles.go:164-167) and set only at audit.go:192; the only other consumer is auditfiles_test.go:79.

resolved.evidence: Same defect as the tester's conditional-requirement finding, fixed together: §2.4 item 3 now states the fact instead of a condition and enumerates the four fields AuditFileInputs retains, so the acceptance is verifiable.

suggestion: Resolve the condition in the spec: state that HeadReader (the field and its audit.go assignment) and GitHeadReader are removed because selectSecurity is their only reader, and that AuditFileInputs keeps Universe/DiffStats/Deleted/TaskFiles.

finding: Removing `AuditFileSelection.Security` breaks the caller chain the spec never mentions. routeChecklist (audit_roles.go:31-56) returns `(spec, sec, maint)` and builds `sec` from `sel.Security` and `maint` from the hardcoded `roleMaintainability`; runAudit (audit.go:216) destructures all three and threads `specItems, secItems, maintItems` into generateRoleAuditPrompts's signature. With the two switch arms deleted, both extra return values and both extra parameters are dead, and the code does not compile with `sel.Security` gone — yet the spec describes only the switch. An implementer must invent the new signatures.

resolved.evidence: §2.1 now states the caller-chain collapse the switch deletion forces: routeChecklist drops its sel argument and its sec/maint return values and produces the spec-coverage checklist alone, generateRoleAuditPrompts drops the secItems and maintItems parameters, and runAudit stops destructuring three values.

suggestion: Add a sentence to §2.1 or §2.2 stating that routeChecklist reduces to producing the spec-coverage checklist only (spec-derived + finding items), that its `sel` argument and the `secItems`/`maintItems` parameters of generateRoleAuditPrompts are dropped, and that every non-spec-coverage role's items are built inside the shared arm via fileCheckItems.

finding: The cost sentence ('Removing the heuristic does not widen the token budget: the shared list is capped at 10 files while the security list was capped at 20, and the per-role file inliner already inlines at most one role's files per audit round') is only true for the repos where the heuristic already matched — i.e. not the repos this release fixes. In the reported PHP case the security role went from 0 emitted prompts to 1: that is one additional sub-agent invocation per audit round, forever, times the required clean rounds; plus ~10 more checklist items and ~10 more NDJSON rows the agent must produce, merge, and read every round even when all PASS. The inliner argument bounds prompt bytes only — every non-inliner role receives named paths and must read the same 10 files itself, so file reads scale with the number of emitted roles, not with the inliner.

resolved.evidence: The false 'does not widen the token budget' claim is gone. §6 Cost states the real delta for exactly the repositories this release fixes — one extra role prompt and sub-agent per round, up to CodeFileCap named files that role reads itself, one result row per file, repeated per required clean round — and keeps the 20-vs-10 bound only for the already-emitting case.

suggestion: Replace the 'does not widen the token budget' claim with the real delta and its justification: in repos where the heuristic emptied the list, an audit round now costs one additional role prompt (one sub-agent), up to 10 named code files that role reads itself, and ~10 extra result rows per round — the price of the role running at all, which is what the release buys. Keep the 20-vs-10 note as the bound on the already-emitting case.

finding: §2.2 defends the deletion only on token budget ("shared list capped at 10 while the security list was capped at 20"), and that same asymmetry is a detection-coverage loss the spec never states: today a keyword-matching file at alphabetical position 11..20 reaches the security lens; after the change every non-spec-coverage role sees only the first 10 universe files, so on any audit with more than 10 changed files a genuinely security-relevant file that sorts late is no longer audited by that lens at all. The release is presented as strictly a fix (§1, §2.1) while it narrows coverage in a common case.

resolved.evidence: §2.4 now states the narrowing rather than only the token argument: a keyword-matching file sorting at alphabetical position 11 through 20 previously reached the security lens and no longer does, with --affected-files and §5.1's role-declared selection named as the levers and the reason the cap is not raised (it would double every emitted role's file list at once).

suggestion: State the trade-off explicitly in §2.2 — uniform routing costs late-sorting files their security lens until §5.1's role-declared file selection lands — and either raise the shared cap to `AuditFileCap` or name the interim workaround (`--affected-files` scoping) so a reader is not surprised.

finding: The rename breaks internal/engine/auditfiles_test.go at compile time and §6 says nothing about it. TestFilterFiles_Maintainability:105-107, TestFilterFiles_DropsBinaryFixturesDeleted:123-125 and TestFilterFiles_DropFirstBackfill:140-145 reference sel.Maintainability and MaintainabilityFileCap (mechanical rename), but TestFilterFiles_Security:76 and the second half of TestFilterFiles_Cap20:67-73 ('security capped at 20') test only the deleted selection and must be DELETED, not renamed — an implementer following §2.3 alone has no instruction. Additionally, §2.3 claims 'the cap value ... unchanged', yet every surviving assertion is written against the constant (require.Len(t, sel.Maintainability, MaintainabilityFileCap)), so changing CodeFileCap from 10 to any other value keeps those tests green; the only thing pinning 10 today is the incidental assert on index [9].

resolved.evidence: §2.8 item 3 distinguishes deletion from renaming: TestFilterFiles_Security and the security half of TestFilterFiles_Cap20 are deleted with the selection, the rest of the file is renamed mechanically. §7 item 6 now asserts CodeFileCap as the literal 10 and AuditFileCap as the literal 20, so the 'cap value unchanged' claim is actually enforced instead of being self-referential.

suggestion: State in §2.3 that TestFilterFiles_Security and the security half of TestFilterFiles_Cap20 are removed with the selection, and that the remaining engine tests are renamed. Add a §6 item asserting CodeFileCap == 10 as a literal (and that spec-coverage still uses AuditFileCap == 20), so the 'cap value unchanged' claim is actually enforced.

finding: §2.4 enumerates the skip outcomes that survive but covers only spec-coverage. A non-spec-coverage role is still skipped with `no-checklist-items` whenever the code-file list is empty, and that is reachable: determineAuditFiles/resolveAuditFiles only exit 4 when nothing is derivable, while filterAuditUniverse can still empty a non-empty universe by dropping binaries, testdata/** and *.golden, and deleted files (auditfiles.go:75-85). So a round whose diff touches only images or fixtures skips every auditor. The spec's headline promise ('every auditor role emits a prompt', test §6.1) silently assumes at least one surviving code file, and no §6 test covers the empty-universe case.

resolved.evidence: §2.7 'The skip outcomes that survive' added, enumerating both reachable no-checklist-items paths — an empty spec-coverage checklist, and an empty shared code-file list after the binary/testdata/.golden/deleted drop rules — and stating that both are reported identically with an unchanged exit code. §7 item 10 tests the second path.

suggestion: Extend §2.4 to name the second surviving skip reason: a non-spec-coverage role is skipped with `no-checklist-items` exactly when the shared code-file list is empty after the drop rules, and state whether that is reported any differently from the spec-coverage skip.

finding: §2.4 pins `no-checklist-items` only for spec-coverage and never states the outcome when the shared code-file list is EMPTY — the universe is empty, or every file is dropped by the binary/testdata/.golden/deleted rules (filterAuditUniverse). In that case every non-spec-coverage role receives zero file_check items and is skipped with `no-checklist-items` — i.e. the release's headline symptom ('the auditor is silently skipped') still occurs, just for a different reason. §6 has no item for it, so the boundary ships untested and undocumented.

resolved.evidence: Same gap as the implementer's unstated-edge-case finding, fixed together: §2.7 states the empty-code-file outcome explicitly and §7 item 10 asserts it with a testdata/.golden affected file, naming every non-spec-coverage role in skipped_roles.

suggestion: Add a sentence to §2.4 stating the empty-code-file outcome explicitly (all non-spec-coverage roles skipped with no-checklist-items, named in skipped_roles) and add a §6 test: audit with --affected-files pointing only at a .golden/testdata path → skipped_roles names every non-spec-coverage role with that reason, exit code unchanged.

finding: §2.4 pins the skip outcome for an empty spec-coverage checklist but never states the corresponding rule for the shared arm: when the code-file list is empty (a docs-only or fixture-only diff, or every universe file dropped as binary/testdata/deleted) every non-spec-coverage role receives zero `file_check` items and is skipped with `no-checklist-items`. That is now the dominant skip path for the majority of roles, and §6 test 1 constrains only the one-affected-file case, so the release's central routing section leaves its most likely empty case unspecified.

resolved.evidence: Same gap as the two other empty-selection findings, fixed together in §2.7 and §7 item 10; the headline promise of §7 item 1 is now scoped to the case where at least one code file survives the drop rules, with the empty case specified separately.

suggestion: Add a sentence to §2.4 stating that a non-spec-coverage role is skipped with `no-checklist-items` exactly when the shared code-file list is empty, and add a test asserting that outcome (and that it names every such role) for a diff whose universe filters to zero code files.

finding: §1 says the defect was reproduced against an ejected `--domain software` corpus, but §3 rewrites only the embedded corpus. A project that already ran `tp init --eject-roles` owns .tp/auditors/security.json and .tp/auditors/maintainability-conventions.json on disk; upgrading tp changes nothing for it, and re-ejecting refuses to overwrite without --force (init.go:140-146), which would also clobber any local edits. §3.4's advisory only fires on a fresh eject, so exactly the reporter's configuration receives none of §3. The spec states no migration path and no notice.

resolved.evidence: §5 Non-Goal 3 added: an ejected corpus is project-owned data tp never rewrites on upgrade, so the reporter's own configuration receives §2 but not §3, and §4's documentation is the notice. A byte-identity staleness hint for superseded defaults is named as possible future work rather than left implicit.

suggestion: State the intended outcome for already-ejected corpora — either explicitly out of scope (with a Non-Goal saying an ejected corpus is project-owned and is not migrated), or specify how a user learns their ejected defaults are stale (e.g. an informational line when an ejected role file is byte-identical to a superseded embedded default).

finding: '`tp init --eject-roles` adds one advisory line to its output' does not say which channel. tp's convention is JSON on stdout when piped and info messages suppressible with --quiet; an advisory appended to the stdout JSON payload would change a machine-parsed output contract for every agent that scripts eject, while an advisory on the info channel costs the agent nothing when it passes --quiet. 'informational output only' resolves file-content-vs-output but not payload-vs-info-channel.

resolved.evidence: §3.4 pins the channel: the advisory goes to the human/info channel alongside the existing success message, is suppressed by --quiet, and adds no key to the eject JSON payload, whose shape stays exactly {ejected, domain}. §7 item 14 asserts both the substring and the unchanged JSON keys.

suggestion: Pin it: the line is an info message on the non-JSON channel (stderr), suppressed by --quiet, and never a field of the eject JSON payload. Add a §6 test asserting the stdout JSON is byte-identical before and after the advisory is introduced.

finding: 'adds one advisory line to its output' has no assertable form: the spec names no stream (runEjectRoles emits both output.Success to the human channel — suppressible by --quiet — and output.JSON({"ejected","domain"}) to stdout), no JSON field name, no exact wording, and no condition. §1 states 'no schema change', but adding a field to the eject JSON IS a schema change, while putting it in output.Success makes it invisible to a piped/--quiet caller and to any JSON assertion. It is also unstated whether the line is emitted for `--domain prose`, where 'language-neutral starting point ... rewrite for your stack' is the wrong claim. §6 item 8 only asserts the byte-identity test still passes; nothing asserts the advisory exists at all.

resolved.evidence: Same gap as the two other §3.4 findings, fixed together: §3.4 now pins the channel, the --quiet behavior, the unchanged JSON shape, and — answering the prose point specifically — states that the wording names no language so the line is emitted for every domain including prose. §7 item 14 asserts it for both domains.

suggestion: Pin the channel and the text: e.g. 'runEjectRoles emits the advisory via output.Success (stderr/TTY info, suppressed by --quiet); the eject JSON payload is unchanged' plus a quoted substring a test can assert. State whether it is domain-conditional. Add a §6 item asserting the substring is present for --domain software (and the intended behavior for prose) and that the JSON keys stay exactly {ejected, domain}.

finding: 'adds one advisory line to its output' never says which output. runEjectRoles (internal/cli/init.go:156-157) ends with an output.Success line plus output.JSON({"ejected": [...], "domain": ...}). An advisory emitted as a new JSON key changes the machine-readable shape (and the existing TestInitEjectRoles_Output contract); emitted via output.Success/Info it goes to the human channel and is suppressed by --quiet. The spec gives neither the channel, nor the wording, nor the --quiet/--json behavior, and §6.8 only asserts the written files are unchanged — nothing pins that the line is emitted at all.

resolved.evidence: Same gap as the two other §3.4 findings, fixed together: §3.4 states the channel, the --quiet behavior and the unchanged {ejected, domain} payload, and §7 item 14 asserts the line is emitted at all rather than only that the written files are unchanged.

suggestion: State the channel (e.g. an informational line alongside the existing success message, no JSON field added), give the literal text or its required substance, say whether --quiet suppresses it, and add a §6 test that the line appears while the `ejected`/`domain` JSON payload is unchanged.

finding: §4 names README.md, skills/tp/SKILL.md and CLAUDE.md, but skills/tp/REFERENCE.md also states the audit routing contract it is about — the `prompts[].role` enum as the fixed three ids and the deterministic item ids `file-sec-<n>`/`file-maint-<n>` — so it will contradict the new routing after this release while remaining a committed, shipped doc.

resolved.evidence: §4 now names skills/tp/REFERENCE.md in the documentation set and states the concrete correction it needs: its documented file-sec-<n>/file-maint-<n> item ids are already wrong against today's code and become file-<role-id>-<slug>.

suggestion: Add skills/tp/REFERENCE.md to §4's documentation set with the same requirement (spec-coverage is the only dedicated checklist source; every other role gets one item per affected code file, with `file-<role-id>-<slug>` item ids), so all four docs state one routing story.

finding: §4 tells the docs to state that `spec-coverage` receives the spec-derived checklist and every other auditor receives one item per affected code file, "with no id treated specially" — but that same sentence, and §2.1, keep `spec-coverage` as an id that selects a distinct behavior. A doc written to §4 literally would be self-contradictory, and a reader cannot predict a role authored with the id `spec-coverage` from it.

resolved.evidence: §4 rephrased to remove the self-contradiction: spec-coverage is the single reserved id with a dedicated checklist source and every other id is routed identically. The absolute 'no id is treated specially' phrasing is deleted from both §4 and the §2.1 claim it echoed.

suggestion: Rewrite the §4 requirement as: `spec-coverage` is the single reserved id with a dedicated checklist source; every other id — built-in, ejected, or user-authored — is routed identically. Drop the absolute "no id treated specially" phrasing and say instead that no id other than `spec-coverage` changes routing.

finding: 'a role named `security` and an identically-authored role named anything else now produce identical checklists for identical inputs' is literally false and contradicts test §6.2. fileCheckItems (audit_roles.go:91-113) embeds the role id in both the item id (`file-<roleID>-<slug>`, where the slug also derives from the role-id-bearing text) and the item text ('Apply the <roleID> role rules to <path>'), so the two checklists differ item by item; §6.2 correctly asserts only equal item count and equal affected-files list.

resolved.evidence: §2.1 reworded to the property that is actually true and testable: the two roles receive the same number of items over the same files in the same order, differing only in the role id that fileCheckItems embeds in each item_id and text, with prompts identical modulo the role id and output path.

suggestion: Reword §2.1 to the property that is actually true and testable: the two roles receive the same number of items over the same files, differing only in the role id embedded in each item's id and text.

finding: The `security` role's file_check item ids are derived from the selected file paths, and its file list changes from the keyword-filtered subset to the shared code list. For a project mid-audit-sequence, the prior-round non-PASS rows replayed into the next prompt (§10.2, renderPriorRoundSection, audit_roles.go:186-203) will reference item ids that no longer exist this round. The existing `legacy` marker only covers rounds recorded before stable ids, so the crossing-the-upgrade case is silently unmarked. The spec does not mention it.

resolved.evidence: §5 Non-Goal 7 added, recording the item-id churn across the upgrade as an accepted consequence: an audit sequence crossing this release replays prior rows whose item ids no longer exist, the auditor re-checks either way, and a new marker is not warranted for a one-release transition.

suggestion: Add a sentence stating the accepted consequence: an in-flight audit sequence's `security` prior rows may not map onto this round's item ids, and whether that is left as-is (the auditor re-checks anyway) or deserves a marker.

finding: §2.3 asserts the rename produces 'no output difference', but the emitted prompt hardcodes the header '## Affected Files (max 20)' (internal/cli/audit_roles.go:237) while every non-spec-coverage role's list is capped at 10 (CodeFileCap). Before this change that header was at least accurate for the security role (cap 20); after §2.2 deletes it, the only role the '20' still describes is spec-coverage. The prompt now overstates the cap for every code-file role and nothing in §6 pins the header against the constant.

resolved.evidence: §2.6 added: the header is rendered from the cap actually applied to that role's list instead of the fixed 'max 20' literal, and when the pre-cap universe held more files than the list shows it also states how many of how many are shown, so a truncated set is never presented as complete. §7 item 9 pins both halves.

suggestion: Either state in §2.3 that the header literal is intentionally left alone (with the caveat that it is now inaccurate for code-file roles), or make it render each role's actual cap; add a §6 assertion that the header's stated number matches the cap applied to that role's list.

finding: §2.3 claims the rename has 'no output difference', but the emitted prompt header is the fixed string '## Affected Files (max 20)' (internal/cli/audit_roles.go:237) while the shared list caps at 10 — and after §2.1 that mismatched header now appears in every non-spec-coverage prompt instead of just one. An auditor sub-agent reading 'max 20' next to 10 files reasonably infers the change set was 10 files and that nothing was truncated, which is exactly wrong when 40 files changed and 30 were dropped by the cap.

resolved.evidence: Same defect as the tester's stale-prompt-literal finding, fixed together in §2.6 — and the silent-truncation half this finding raised is what drove the 'N of M shown' addition, since a cap that drops files without saying so is exactly the kind of silent narrowing tp refuses elsewhere.

suggestion: Either render the header from the cap actually applied to that role's list, or state in §2.3 that the header is a known pre-existing inaccuracy left untouched by the rename — and, if the cap is now silent truncation for most roles, say whether the prompt must disclose 'N of M changed files shown'.

finding: Rewriting the embedded default focus lines changes the prompts a default-corpus project emits, but ComputeRolesHash returns the `builtin` sentinel whenever a phase has no user role files (internal/engine/rolehash.go), so `roles_stale` stays false and an in-flight audit sequence's recorded rounds are not marked as having run under different instructions. There is precedent for this being intentional (v0.25.0 §5.2: the regression role's content ships with a tp release and is excluded from the hash), but this spec never states it, and v0.25.0 §5.4 took the opposite honesty stance for the eject case.

resolved.evidence: §3.5 added, recording that the embedded prompt rewrite deliberately leaves roles_hash at the builtin sentinel, citing the v0.25.0 §5.2 precedent that release-shipped content is excluded because a tp upgrade is already a visible event, and naming ejection as the way a project gets its role content hashed.

suggestion: State in §3 that the prompt change ships with the tp release and therefore does not flip `roles_hash` off `builtin`, citing the v0.25.0 §5.2 precedent — so the omission is recorded as a decision rather than read as an oversight.

finding: No §6 item covers §4. The defect this release fixes is precisely a documented-contract/behavior mismatch, and this repo has precedent for pinning exactly that kind of claim with an assertion test (the .golangci.yml gofmt guard test added in v0.31.1). §4's requirement — that README.md, skills/tp/SKILL.md and CLAUDE.md state the two-arm routing and drop any claim that a role id selects behavior — is therefore unverifiable at gate time and can silently rot back.

resolved.evidence: §7 item 13 added: a guard test asserting README.md, skills/tp/SKILL.md and skills/tp/REFERENCE.md each state the two-arm routing rule and that none still describes a special file list or item-id scheme for security or maintainability-conventions — the same guard-test pattern v0.31.1 used for the .golangci.yml formatters section.

suggestion: Add a §6 item: a guard test asserting that README.md and skills/tp/SKILL.md each contain the routing sentence (spec-coverage → spec-derived checklist; every other auditor → one item per affected code file) and that no doc file still states that `security` or `maintainability-conventions` receive a special file list.

finding: Non-Goal 4 defers per-spec role activation to v0.32.0, but this release makes every non-spec-coverage role emit unconditionally — the security role that a project may have been happily (if accidentally) not paying for now costs a sub-agent round every audit round, and the spec names no way to decline it before v0.32.0. A reader hitting the added cost has to rediscover the existing levers themselves.

resolved.evidence: §5 Non-Goal 5 now names today's levers alongside the deferral: eject the corpus and omit or rewrite the role file, or narrow the role's work with a tp.audit_roles frontmatter focus override, so a reader hitting the added cost before v0.32.0 does not have to rediscover them.

suggestion: Add one sentence to Non-Goal 4 naming today's levers: eject the corpus (`tp init --eject-roles`) and omit or rewrite the role file, or narrow the set with the `tp.audit_roles` frontmatter override. One line here saves every affected project an investigation.

finding: Item 7's deny-list guard is not specified precisely enough to write once and trust: it says 'no embedded default auditor focus line' — leaving open which corpora (software only, or prose's soundness.json / spec-coverage.json too), which fields (only `focus`, so a Go idiom reintroduced into `instructions` or `title` still ships — note maintainability-conventions.json's instructions already say 'idiomatic'), whether matching is case-sensitive (`camelCase` vs `camelcase`), and whether reviewer roles are in scope (§3.1 exempts them, so the guard would not catch a Go idiom added to a default reviewer later). The token `packages` is also an ordinary English word that would false-positive on a future prose role.

resolved.evidence: §7 item 12 fully specified: it walks internal/engine/corpus/*/auditors/*.json, scans both focus lines and the instructions string, matches case-insensitively, and states reviewer roles are deliberately out of scope with §3.1 as the reason. Bare 'packages' was dropped as an ordinary English word and replaced by the phrase 'lowercase packages'.

suggestion: Specify the guard exactly: which directories it walks (internal/engine/corpus/*/auditors/*.json), which fields it scans (focus AND instructions), case-insensitive matching, and the literal deny-list. If reviewers are out of scope, say so in §6 item 7 so the omission is deliberate rather than accidental.

finding: §6 test 7's deny-list (`%w`, `0o600`, `camelCase`, `_ = err`, `packages`) does not cover everything §3.1 names as the defect: §3.1 also cites the tp-specific phrasing "Files written by the tool", which no deny-list token catches, and the guard is scoped to focus lines only while a role's `instructions` field is equally part of the emitted prompt. Meanwhile `packages` is an ordinary English word that a legitimately language-neutral line could contain, so the guard is simultaneously under- and over-inclusive relative to §3.1's stated criterion.

resolved.evidence: Same guard as the tester's underspecified-guard finding, fixed together: the deny-list now also carries 'files written by the tool' (the tp-specific phrasing §3.1 names but no token caught) and 0o644 and goroutine, and the guard scans instructions as well as focus, so it matches §3.1's stated criterion in both directions.

suggestion: Align §6.7 with §3.1: apply the guard to both `focus` and `instructions` of every embedded default auditor, and pick tokens that are unambiguously language-specific (`%w`, `0o600`, `0o644`, `camelCase`, `_ = err`, `goroutine`), dropping bare `packages` or narrowing it to `lowercase packages`.
